title: Last words
hookLine: if la ilaha illallah is the whole point, why would anyone need to be prompted to say it?
tomorrow: who is the soul at peace, and when does it hear that call?

cards: Lists of well-known last words get passed around online: funny ones, brave ones, strange ones.
A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud answers yesterday's question with one sentence: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah, there is no god but Allah, enters Paradise. Simple enough.
But a hadith in Sahih Muslim adds an odd instruction. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told people to prompt their dying with these words. Prompt them?
If the sentence is the whole point, why would anyone need help saying it?

teach.b: Because the end isn't always clear-headed. Pain, medicine, exhaustion, fear: the words you've said all your life can be hard to find at the door. So the people by the bed help.
The word for this is talqin, prompting. And here's the second half of the puzzle.

Scholars who wrote about it, such as al-Nawawi, advise saying it softly near the person, not ordering them to repeat it, and not pressing again once they've said it, unless they speak of other things.
The prompt is a kindness, not a test. That's why the sentence is so short. La ilaha illallah is in the call to prayer, inside the prayer, in dhikr counted on the fingers.
A life of saying it is a rehearsal, so that at the end it's already on the tongue. Some families say it quietly in a hospital room, not as an exam, but as company.
In the hadith, then, the last words aren't left to chance. The people who love you help you find them.

how: Muslims at the bedside of someone dying often say la ilaha illallah softly near them (talqin), without pressing them to repeat it; across life the phrase is said in the call to prayer, in prayer and in dhikr.

o: a prayer an imam says over someone after they die
the sentence hoped for at the end, practiced over a life
a final message a person leaves for their family

games.q: what's inside the teaching — tap the pairs.
p: there is no god but Allah
prompt your dying with these words
a soft prompt, not a test

s: only the last sentence matters, not the life before it
a life of saying it is the rehearsal, so it's already on the tongue at the end.
a hadith in Sahih Muslim tells people to prompt their dying with la ilaha illallah
the right way to prompt is to have the person repeat it again and again
scholars such as al-Nawawi advise saying it softly nearby and not pressing once it's been said.

games.q: in a hospital room, a relative keeps telling your drowsy great-uncle, 'say it! say la ilaha illallah!' again and again. what does the teaching on talqin suggest?
o: say it softly near him, and don't keep pressing.
keep going until he says it clearly a few times.
stay quiet; prompting isn't part of the tradition.
games.why: the hadith says prompt them; scholars like al-Nawawi say do it gently and don't press. a kindness, not a test.

practice: Where you can, say la ilaha illallah softly, once, then again at the pace of your breath, listening to it instead of rushing.
If you're learning about Islam rather than practicing it, simply listen to the shape of the words as someone else might say them, quietly, at a bedside.

wordCard.voice: Last words: the sentence a Muslim hopes to say at the end, la ilaha illallah, rehearsed over a lifetime and gently prompted by the people nearby.

orig.note: Arabic: there is no god but Allah; the first half of the shahada.

carryVoice: Three words to keep: my last words, already practiced, already on the tongue. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 3116: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah will enter Paradise
Sahih Muslim 916: prompt your dying with la ilaha illallah
al-Nawawi, al-Adhkar, on talqin: say it gently near the dying person, without pressing, and do not repeat once said unless they speak of other things
